sources.news_title: Carney Backs Closer Canada-EU Alliance as Brussels Floats First-Ever ‘Associate Membership’
sources.text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney endorsed a proposed new relationship that could make Canada the European Union’s first associate member, calling for deeper economic, defense and technological integration while maintaining Canadian sovereignty.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
STRASBOURG, France — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney threw his support Thursday behind a proposal to forge an unprecedented new relationship between Canada and the European Union, potentially establishing his country as the bloc’s first “associate member” as Ottawa seeks to diversify its economic and security relationships beyond the United States.
Addressing the European Parliament in Strasbourg, Carney welcomed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal for a level of Canada-EU integration that does not currently exist under the bloc’s treaties. Although the exact legal and institutional meaning of associate membership has yet to be established, Carney outlined a broad partnership covering trade, defense, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, energy, space, research and financial services.
Carney framed closer European ties as a means of increasing Canada’s ability to withstand economic and geopolitical pressure without creating another competing global power center.
“I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival — only with better manners,” Carney said. “We do not seek power to dominate others.”
Instead, Carney said Canada wants greater economic and strategic resilience so that no individual country can control Canadian markets, weaken its sovereignty or dictate its choices. Reuters reported that Carney defended Canada’s right to determine its own international partnerships while advocating deeper cooperation with Europe.
The proposal comes amid continuing tensions between Ottawa and Washington over tariffs and other economic issues. President Donald Trump criticized the idea before Carney’s address, suggesting that an EU arrangement with Canada could constitute a “hostile act” and warning that he could impose additional tariffs on Europe if he concluded the partnership was directed against U.S. interests.
Von der Leyen unveiled the associate membership concept Wednesday during her State of the European Union address, with Carney attending in Strasbourg. She proposed taking the Canada-EU relationship to “the highest level possible” and described a future arrangement built around a broader “common prosperity and economic security space.”
The proposed status would be new. Associate membership is not presently an established category within EU treaties, meaning its powers, obligations and legal structure would have to be negotiated and defined before such an arrangement could take effect.
Carney received an enthusiastic reception in the European Parliament, where lawmakers approached him before his speech, and members gave him a standing ovation. Von der Leyen and Carney embraced in the chamber following her proposal for the closer relationship.
The initiative represents the latest step in a broader Canadian effort to reduce the country’s economic dependence on its southern neighbor.
Canada’s economy has been closely integrated with the United States for generations, and roughly 70% of Canadian exports currently go to the U.S. Carney’s government has sought additional markets as it responds to U.S. tariffs and other trade pressure while rejecting demands that Ottawa says would infringe on Canadian sovereignty.
Trump has also repeatedly talked about Canada becoming the 51st U.S. state, remarks that have become part of the broader strain between Washington and Ottawa. Carney has responded by emphasizing Canadian sovereignty and seeking stronger economic and security ties with countries outside the United States.
Europe has taken a different approach in its own trade confrontation with Washington, accepting tariffs of as much as 15% on many exports to the United States rather than proceeding with broader retaliatory measures.
Carney has repeatedly argued that countries outside the world’s largest powers need to cooperate rather than negotiate individually against states capable of exerting substantially greater economic leverage.
Speaking at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Carney warned about the consequences of smaller and middle powers confronting dominant countries individually.
“We negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered,” Carney said.
The Canadian government’s move toward Europe was already underway before the associate membership proposal.
Canada officially joined the European Union’s Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, initiative in February, becoming the first non-European country to participate. The program is part of Europe’s effort to expand defense readiness and provides a framework for joint procurement as European governments increase military spending. The SAFE instrument can provide up to 150 billion euros in financing for defense-related investment.
The two sides also launched a broader strategic partnership in 2025 covering areas including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and digital infrastructure and established a security and defense partnership consolidating cooperation between Canada, the EU and its member states.
The European Union is already Canada’s second-largest trading partner for goods and services. Canada’s government reported approximately $178 billion in bilateral goods and services trade with the EU in 2025. The bloc is also Canada’s second-largest source of foreign direct investment after the United States.
Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the European Union, said Ottawa is not seeking full membership in the EU, which would involve transferring some national decision-making authority to European institutions.
Instead, Wilkinson said Canada wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to Europe while simultaneously strengthening the country’s independence.
That distinction leaves substantial negotiations ahead. Neither Canada nor the EU has defined whether associate membership would provide participation in portions of the European single market, require Canada to adopt additional EU regulations, provide access to specific institutions or establish new decision-making mechanisms.
EU officials have also indicated that the concept remains at an early stage. Reuters reported that some European diplomats have questioned how the new status would work because it has not yet been formally established within the bloc’s existing structure.
Carney nevertheless used Thursday’s speech to identify a sweeping range of areas where he wants the relationship expanded, including critical minerals needed for advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence, energy security, defense procurement, digital commerce, research, space technology and financial services.
Canada and the EU are scheduled to have another opportunity to define those ambitions next month.
Carney will host European leaders in Montreal for a Canada-EU summit Oct. 29-30. The European Council has confirmed the dates and location of the meeting, while the Canadian government has said the summit will build on the expanding relationship between the two sides.
The changing Canada-U.S. relationship has become an important factor in the European outreach, according to political scholars following the negotiations.
“The policies and rhetoric of the Trump administration are clearly pushing both Canada and the EU to imagine a world without strong U.S. leadership and to act accordingly,” Daniel Béland, a political-science professor at McGill University in Montreal, said.
Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said European governments have historically viewed Canada as possessing unusual insight into Washington because of the two countries’ extensive economic, cultural and political ties.
“Carney’s shrewdness in dealing with Trump has captured Europe’s attention,” Wiseman said.
Wiseman said Carney’s willingness to resist demands from Washington rather than quickly reach an accommodation has contributed to European interest in strengthening relations with Ottawa.
Béland also said Carney’s decision not to center his European Parliament speech explicitly on Trump did not mean Washington was absent from the calculations surrounding the address.
“He knows that, beyond Europe, the world will be watching, including the White House,” Béland said.
Carney’s government has stressed that closer ties with Europe are intended to increase Canadian independence rather than substitute dependence on one major economic partner for dependence on another.
With the proposed associate status still undefined, negotiations leading into the October summit will determine whether von der Leyen’s proposal develops into a formal new category of EU partnership and what economic, security and political commitments Canada and Europe would make under such an arrangement.

Canada welcomes EU proposal to become 'associate member'
- Published
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the European Union's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member", calling for closer cooperation on defence, critical minerals and energy security.
Carney told the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
His comments came a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to Canada's associate membership, a status that does not currently exist.
US President Donald Trump earlier called the idea "laughable" and threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".
Canada and the US are locked in an escalating trade dispute, with each side imposing tit-for-tat tariffs after bilateral talks collapsed last month.
"Today our societies are being battered by new storms," Carney said during his address, naming them as climate change, "the erosion of democratic norms" and the "weaponisation of trade".
"Economic integration is now being weaponised, tariffs being used to exert pressure," he said.
"Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited."
He said a Canada-EU alliance would create a "beacon for other democracies", while stressing the two sides were not seeking to form a new power bloc.
"I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival - only with better manners," he told MEPs.
"This is about sovereignty, our ability to live as we wish. We do not seek power to dominate others."
Asked about the proposal on Wednesday, Trump told reporters: "If I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things.
"If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility."
Responding to Trump's comments at a press conference following his address, Carney said: "This alliance is a positive process, that's my response to the American president."
"Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak, no-one is going to dictate our culture, or with whom we can strike agreements internationally," he added.
Carney said Canada was "not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member of the European Union", describing the proposal as a "different framework".
- What could EU associate member status mean for Canada? 
  - Published7 hours ago
- Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump 
  - Published1 day ago
- EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member' 
  - Published22 hours ago
Speaking at the European Parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen said she wanted Canada to become the EU's first associate member, with closer cooperation in areas such as manufacturing, technology, defence, energy critical minerals and economic security.
It is unclear exactly what that relationship would look like because the "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement.
Any new arrangement would require the agreement of all 27 EU member states, with some governments having previously expressed reservations about creating a new form of membership.
The EU and Canada already have a free-trade agreement, and cooperate in areas including trade, defence and research.
In his address, Carney said Canada and Europe could strengthen their "strategic autonomy" through "deep co-operation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals".
He said Canada could supply liquefied natural gas and hydrogen to support European energy security, while benefiting from Europe's expertise in clean-energy technologies.
He also proposed pooling technological resources and deepening "people to people ties", including allowing young people to "work, study and live where they want on either side of the Atlantic" through Canada joining the EU's Erasmus+ programme.
Carney described the proposed relationship as "a unique, positive approach that we will define together".
He added that there would be a debate and a vote in the Canadian parliament on the proposals, but emphasised the two sides were still at the "start of a road".
A Canada-EU summit is due to take place in Montreal at the end of October, where Carney said they would "drill down the details".

"Europe and Canada are stronger together": Mark Carney welcomes historic offer for Ottawa to become first "Associate Member"
Strasbourg [France], September 17 (ANI): Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday (local time) delivered a landmark address to the European Parliament, warmly welcoming European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s historic proposal for Canada to become the European Union’s very first Associate Member.
Addressing lawmakers in Strasbourg a day after von der Leyen pitched the groundbreaking initiative during her State of the Union address, Carney embraced the vision of a transformed transatlantic bond.
Welcoming the initiative, Carney described the partnership between Canada and the EU as a proactive model for global democratic governance. He characterised it as a resilient alliance dedicated to upholding international law and ensuring its agenda is not dictated by outside forces.
"A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies, an alliance not defined by what we oppose, but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability," the Canadian PM said.
"An alliance that builds resilience for what it allows us to do; for our citizens and our citizens to do for themselves; an alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices, an alliance open enough that others can join, an alliance principled enough that our strength reinforces international law rather than seeks to replace it," he added.
Beyond trade, defence capabilities, and raw economic leverage, Carney placed significant emphasis on social integration and youth mobility, advocating for seamless transatlantic opportunities.
"An alliance for the future is a unique, positive approach that we will define together, building on our common strengths and based on our shared values," he declared. "We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to work, study, and live where they want on either side of the Atlantic."
After von der Leyen proposed moving beyond the existing Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or CETA, between Canada and the EU towards a broader strategic partnership, Carney thanked the EU leadership for "our Strategic Partnership Agreement struck last June," noting that they are "developing that and deepening it."
He noted that "yesterday, President von der Leyen spoke of moving beyond CETA to an alliance for the future, opening the door to Canada to become the European Union's first associate member," framing the offer as a pivotal moment for democratic nations seeking shared stability.
Regarding the European Commission President's remarks about "a new European corporation on critical raw materials," he highlighted that "Canada has deposits of over 34 critical minerals, and we are among the top producers of the 10 most essential for the energy transition."
"Our alliance can help fill Europe's need for reliable supply, Canada's desire for advanced processing capabilities, and our common objective to complete value chains in the transition and our defence," he emphasised.
Furthermore, Carney drew a sharp line between strategic defence and aggressive geopolitics, clarifying that Ottawa and Brussels are not seeking to create a confrontational geopolitical bloc.
"I also want to be precise about what I am not proposing. I'm not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great power rival only with better manners," Carney affirmed.
"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one, no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law," he added.
Firmly rejecting the notion that closer cooperation equates to a surrender of independence, Carney emphasised that the initiative is designed to defend national self-determination against external pressures.
"Deepening and widening our relationship will strengthen our sovereignty, improve affordability and opportunity and security for our citizens, while safeguarding our ability to live our lives as we choose," Carney stated.
The Prime Minister stressed that the proposed partnership is rooted in genuine autonomy rather than transactional self-sufficiency.
"The economics of this are clear. The leverage of the powerful in an exploitative relationship collapses well before complete independence is achieved, because diversity confers advantage. The objective is not self-sufficiency; it's collective resilience. It's this mutual advantage that's at the core of the case for a deeper partnership between Canada and Europe," he stated.
He added that true national strength depends directly on the capacity to withstand external global shocks:
"This is about sovereignty. Our ability to live as we wish. It's about the freedoms we must fight for every day. Because sovereignty requires resilience, the ability to withstand shocks. Canada and Europe are each strong. Europe and Canada are stronger together."
Carney reminded lawmakers that the foundation connecting Canada and Europe extends far beyond commercial agreements:
"The depth of our bonds, those which unite us, cannot be measured by trade or what is written in treaties alone; our bonds are deeply rooted in our lands."
"We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom, and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication."
Likening the current era of geopolitical fragmentation, weaponised trade, and economic instability to a gathering storm, Carney called for structural unity.
"We are bound by an affinity, elective, chosen, renewed, and stronger for being so. Today, our societies are being battered by new storms," Carney observed. "A single tree will come down in it. A forest will not."
He closed by invoking a broader vision of economic justice and environmental responsibility:
"We hold common values for which we have always fought, and in whose defence we must always remain vigilant. We believe that a strong economy is not an end in itself, but a means to a just society. We are committed stewards of our natural heritage."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday invited Canada to become the European Union's first "associate member", signalling a push by Brussels and Ottawa to deepen economic and strategic ties amid growing uncertainty in transatlantic trade relations.
"I invite Canada to be the first associate member of the EU," von der Leyen said during her State of the Union speech here.
Canada is not eligible for full EU membership under the bloc's treaties, which restrict membership to European states.
Against that backdrop, the proposal for an "associate member" represents a possible new framework for closer cooperation between Canada and the 27-member bloc.
Following her remarks, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney formally applied for Ottawa's membership to join the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a defence coalition of 10 Northern European NATO nations.
According to a statement issued by the Office of the Prime Minister of Canada on Wednesday following Carney's talks with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Liverpool, the two leaders discussed strengthening their defence and security partnership, with Carney announcing Ottawa's formal application to join the JEF and welcoming the UK's support for Canada's participation.
"Prime Minister Carney announced that Canada has formally applied to join the Joint Expeditionary Force and welcomed the UK’s support for Canada’s participation in this important initiative," the statement read.
The Canadian and European leaders are also due to meet later in October at a summit in Montreal, where issues including trade, defence, energy, critical minerals, technology and Arctic cooperation are expected to feature prominently.
The proposal comes as Canada and the EU seek to strengthen economic resilience amid heightened uncertainty in global trade, including recent tensions between Ottawa and Washington under US President Donald Trump's trade policies. (ANI)

The two sides have also discussed closer cooperation on energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and digital trade.
“The policies and rhetoric of the Trump administration are clearly pushing both Canada and the EU to imagine a world without strong U.S. leadership and to act accordingly,” said Daniel Béland, a political-science professor at McGill University in Montreal.
Nelson Wiseman, a professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Carney’s handling of Trump has heightened European interest in the Canadian leader.
“Carney’s shrewdness in dealing with Trump has captured Europe’s attention,” Wiseman said.
Wiseman said Europeans have long regarded Canada as a country that understands the United States particularly well because of their deep economic and political ties. Carney’s willingness to resist Trump rather than quickly accept Washington’s demands has reinforced that perception, he said.
Béland said Carney may avoid naming Trump on Thursday while leaving little doubt about the target of his broader argument.
“He knows that, beyond Europe, the world will be watching, including the White House,” Béland said.

Mark Carney welcomes proposal for Canada to be EU’s first associate member after Trump slams ‘hostile act’

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday welcomed a proposal for Canada to become the European Union’s first associate member, but said he did not mean for a closer alliance to create a new bloc that would rival the world’s great powers.
The remarks came after President Donald Trump suggested the proposed arrangement could be a “hostile act” and threatened heavy tariffs on Europe if he judged its intentions to be unfriendly. Trump also called the idea “laughable.”
“We welcome this ambition,” Carney told the European Parliament of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal, unveiled Wednesday.
Carney said plainly what he was proposing: deeper Canada-Europe integration across trade, defense, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, energy, space, research and financial services to make both sides less vulnerable to economic and geopolitical pressure.
“I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival — only with better manners,” he said. “We do not seek power to dominate others.”
Carney said the goal instead is to build Canada’s resilience so that no country can control its markets, undermine its sovereignty or dictate its choices.
For generations, Canada built its economy around integration with the United States.
Trump’s tariffs, demands for economic concessions and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state are now driving Ottawa to reduce that dependence and seek a deeper economic, security and political relationship across the Atlantic.
Europe offers Canada another path
Von der Leyen proposed making Canada the EU’s first associate member — a status that does not currently exist in the bloc’s treaties and would have to be created.
She said Europe wants to take its relationship with Canada to “the highest level possible.”
Carney, sitting in the front row of the European Parliament chamber, nodded and rose to embrace von der Leyen as lawmakers gave the proposal a standing ovation.
This time, Europe is offering Canada another path.
Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU should move beyond their existing free trade agreement and create an “Alliance for the Future” encompassing a “common prosperity and economic security space.”
Carney will host EU leaders for a Canada-EU summit in Montreal on Oct. 29-30, where the two sides are expected to discuss the proposed new relationship in more detail.
Canada sends roughly 70% of its exports to the United States, making it highly exposed to Trump’s tariffs. Ottawa has retaliated and rejected demands Carney says threaten Canadian sovereignty.
Europe took a different path, shelving retaliation and accepting tariffs of up to 15% on most EU exports to the US.
Carney has rallied ‘middle powers’
Carney has repeatedly urged middle powers to resist that kind of economic coercion. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, he warned that when countries negotiate alone with a dominant power, “we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered.”
Trump rebuked him the next day.
Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the EU, said Wednesday that Canada is not seeking full EU membership because that would require surrendering some sovereignty.
Instead, Ottawa wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to Europe while increasing Canada’s independence.
Exactly what associate membership would mean remains to be negotiated.
Canada has already taken a major step toward European integration.
This year it became the first non-European country to join the EU’s $173-billion SAFE defense procurement program, giving Canadian companies access to joint procurement as Europe increases defense spending.
The two sides have also discussed closer cooperation on energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and digital trade.
“The policies and rhetoric of the Trump administration are clearly pushing both Canada and the EU to imagine a world without strong US leadership and to act accordingly,” said Daniel Béland, a political-science professor at McGill University in Montreal.
Nelson Wiseman, a professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Carney’s handling of Trump has heightened European interest in the Canadian leader.
“Carney’s shrewdness in dealing with Trump has captured Europe’s attention,” Wiseman said.
Washington will be watching
Wiseman said Europeans have long regarded Canada as a country that understands the United States particularly well because of their deep economic and political ties.
Carney’s willingness to resist Trump rather than quickly accept Washington’s demands has reinforced that perception, he said.
Béland said Carney may avoid naming Trump on Thursday while leaving little doubt about the target of his broader argument.
“He knows that, beyond Europe, the world will be watching, including the White House,” Béland said.

sources.news_title: Carney 'welcomes' ambition to make Canada first EU associate member
sources.text:
STRASBOURG — An enhanced partnership with the European Union will be debated and voted on in Canada's Parliament, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday following his address to the EU in France.
Carney's speech came one day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen used her state of the union address to the European Parliament to open the door to Canada becoming what she called the first "associate member" of the EU.
Carney said he welcomed the move, but during a news conference in Strasbourg, France, following the speech, he also said Canadian members of Parliament will be given the chance to debate and vote on whatever alliance is ultimately proposed.
"Yes, we will have a series of debates, I'm sure, in Parliament, relevant committees, and ultimately there will be a vote in the Canadian Parliament for the final structure of the alliance that we're working on," Carney said, while standing alongside Roberta Metsola, president of the European Parliament.
"The next important point is the summit, European-Canada summit in Montreal at the 29th and 30th of October, but it will all roll out transparently. It's an exciting time because this is an opportunity to speak for Canada. Make Canada stronger, more sovereign, more independent, more prosperous, more sustainable."
A similar debate will happen in the European Parliament.
"We look forward and positively at new opportunities with allies such as Canada, with whom we have had partnerships and alliances, call them what you will, for hundreds of years," Metsola said.
"The overwhelmingly positive reaction of members in plenary just a few moments ago will be reflected in a similar reaction in the committees. Of that, I have no doubt."
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez reacted to Carney's speech by sharing a picture on social media of the EU flag with a red maple leaf just off to the left of the circle of 12 yellow stars. The circle is meant to represent unity and harmony among Europe's people.
Carney said Canadians embrace the idea of a stronger relationship with the EU.
"Polling shows an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties,” he said in his address Thursday.
In her speech on Wednesday, von der Leyen was the first to use the specific term "associate member", which is not something that currently exists within the EU, and Canadian officials quickly downplayed the "associate member" label.
Carney said Thursday the "nomenclature" of a new partnership would be determined by the EU but the substance of the arrangement is more important than its name.
That substance is still being developed, but Carney said Canada and Europe should forge deeper ties on critical minerals, defence, artificial intelligence and energy security.
He said the two partners should look at allowing young people to live, work and study on either side of the Atlantic, and creating an integrated market for financial services.
Metsola said this could include Canada joining Erasmus+, a program that facilities student exchanges between member countries.
"If you ask our young people what they associate the European Union with, I would tell you Erasmus is the first thing they mentioned. Horizon is the second thing they mention in terms of opportunities that with Canada could only get bigger," she said.
Horizon Europe is an EU program that funds various research and innovation projects. The program's budget for 2021-2027 is about $150 billion.
Carney did not mention U.S. President Donald Trump by name in his speech, though he alluded to strained relations between both Canada and Europe and the American administration.
"We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy, share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication," Carney said.
"We hold common values, for which we have always fought, and in whose defence we must always remain vigilant."
Trump said Wednesday he views the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU as a possible "hostile act" and threatened to impose more tariffs on Europe.
Carney said a deeper alliance will make Canada a "better partner with the United States."
"Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak, no one going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally," Carney said.
That was a nod to the recent breakdown in trade talks between Canada and the United States. Carney suspended negotiations just before a U.S.-set tariff deadline in August, and he said the U.S. had made demands Canada refused, including restrictions on Canada's protections for French, and on its ability to make trade deals with other countries.
In his address, Carney also sketched out the limits of the proposed arrangement with the EU.
"I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival — only with better manners," he said.
"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law."
After Carney's speech, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre shared a video on social media of his Wednesday caucus address from Penticton, B.C. In it, he said Canadians should decide the future direction of the country.
"We will continue to support co-operation with our European allies, of course, that is the Conservative tradition ... The prime minister, however, needs to get his story straight. He says he wants a possible associate membership or a unique alliance or whatever else he is secretly negotiating with the EU," Poilievre said in his speech.
"But Conservatives are clear. While we support free trade and continued NATO co-operation with our European allies, Conservatives say no EU taxes, no EU laws, and no EU open border policies on immigration in Canada."
Ten of 27 EU countries still haven't ratified a trade deal with Canada that has been in place provisionally for nine years. Canadian businesses have not taken up market access provided to them in Europe to the same extent that European industries have in Canada.
Carney received standing ovations at the beginning and end of his speech from about two-thirds of the European parliamentarians.
Terry Reintke, co-leader of the Greens in the European Parliament said the day before Carney's speech that she hoped to see him more often in the Parliament. She wore a Sidney Crosby Team Canada jersey as she sat in the front row for Carney's speech.
The Greens hold seven per cent of the seats in the EU Parliament.
Not all parliamentarians were as receptive. As Carney approached the podium to begin his speech, one of the European parliamentarians welcomed him with a chant of "USA, USA."
The prime minister chuckled in response.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 17, 2026.
— With files from David Baxter in Ottawa
Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

sources.news_title: Carney says Canada will decide its own partnerships after Trump calls EU proposal ‘laughable’
sources.text:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday welcomed the European Union's ambition to make Ottawa an associate member of the 27-nation bloc and said Canadian lawmakers would ultimately vote on the final structure of the alliance.
"Canada and Europe are each strong. Europe and Canada are stronger together," Carney told EU lawmakers in Strasbourg, France.
Canada's prime minister did not name President Donald Trump in his speech, but he nodded to his U.S. counterpart's use of tariffs by saying, "Economic integration is now being weaponized — tariffs being used to exert pressure."
Speaking in French, Carney continued: "Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited."
His comments come shortly after Trump described the prospect of Canada becoming the first associate member of the EU as "laughable" and threatened the bloc with tariffs if he deemed the move to be a "hostile act."
Speaking to reporters in North Carolina, Trump called Canada a "terrible trade partner" and said the U.S. could even "stop trading with Europe on many things" if the EU moves ahead with its plan. "If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe," Trump said.
The Trump administration recently increased tariffs on Canadian goods, prompting Canada to respond with levies of its own. Carney has pledged to impose reciprocal tariffs on U.S. goods dollar for dollar.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday that the 27-nation bloc wanted to bring the relationship with Canada "to the highest level possible."
Addressing Carney, who was in attendance for the EU chief's state of the union speech, von der Leyen said she would like to work with him "on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union."
Associate membership doesn't currently exist as a formal category under EU treaties, and any such arrangement would need to be created and ratified by member states.
"This alliance is a positive process; that's my response to the American president. A stronger, more resilient, more sovereign Canada will be a more effective partner with the United States," Carney told reporters at a news conference shortly after his speech.
"Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak, no one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally," he added.
'We do not seek power to dominate others'
The EU has previously been reluctant to entertain the prospect of flexible membership categories, notably when earlier in the year, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz pushed for the EU to consider associate membership for Ukraine.
Nonetheless, von der Leyen's backing for Canada to receive associate membership with the EU signals a major deepening of ties between Ottawa and Brussels and comes at a time when Canada is locked in a bitter trade war with the U.S.
Asked whether Canadian lawmakers would be able to debate and vote on the future relationship between Canada and the EU, Carney said: "Of course, there will be debates, plural, not just a single debate, and there will be a vote in the Canadian Parliament. Absolutely, that is clear, but at this particular juncture, we are at the start of a road."
Carney also sought to make clear that a closer relationship between the EU and Canada would bolster collective resilience and "create a beacon" for other democracies.
"Now, I also want to be precise about what I am not proposing, I'm not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great power rival, only with better manners," Carney said.
"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one, no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law," he added.
Carney meets Burnham
The EU and Canada already have a free trade agreement, one that eliminated 99% of all tariff lines when it provisionally came into force in 2017. The pact is known as the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or CETA.

sources.text:
Canada's Carney welcomes associate status idea in EU speech
September 17, 2026
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has said he welcomes the "ambition" of a European Union proposal to make the country the bloc's first associate member.
Carney made the remarks while addressing the European Parliament on Thursday, in a speech that focused on Canada's and the EU's shared security and economic interests.
In an address in which Carney spoke in English, French and German, the Canadian prime minister lauded European culture and values of democracy, freedom and human rights, which he said Canada shares.
"We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defense of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication," the Canadian leader told the chamber, to applause.
Europe and Canada are 'stronger together', Carney tells EU Parliament
"We hold common values for which we have always fought and in whose defense we must always remain vigilant," he said.
"Europe and Canada are each strong," he said. But he added that "Europe and Canada are even stronger together."
"I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival — only with better manners," he said. "We do not seek power to dominate others," he added, in a thinly veiled reference to the US.
"The objective is not self-sufficiency, it's collective resilience," Carney said.
His speech to European lawmakers comes as the EU and Canada look to strengthen their ties amid a growing rift between Canada and its southern neighbor and main trading partner, the US.
Ties between Canada and the US have hit a historic low in recent months, with the North American neighbors locked in an escalating trade war since Carney and US President Donald Trump failed to agree on a deal this summer.
EU defends Canada alliance plan after Trump tariffs threat
On Wednesday, the European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU was willing to make Canada its first-ever "associate member," days after the Wall Street Journal reported that Carney was exploring an "associate membership" with the bloc — a position that does not currently exist. Carney has acknowledged that "associate membership" still needs to be defined.
During her State of the EU address, von der Leyen said the bloc needed to adapt to an "openly hostile world" marked by aggressive power politics and "frayed relationships," the latter a clear nod to the turbulent ties between Brussels and Washington since Trump returned to the White House.
Prior to his visit this week, Carney had confirmed that he wanted to establish a "unique alliance" between Canada and the EU.
"We share the same values, we have the same priorities and we have very complementary strengths," the prime minister said.
Trump on Wednesday slammed the EU's plans to make Canada an associate member.
"If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things," Trump told reporters en route to an event in North Carolina. The US president also described the prospect of Canada joining the EU as "laughable."
How did the US-Canada relationship come to this?
Ties between Canada and the US have plummeted since Trump began his second term in January 2025. He has targeted Canada with tariffs and suggested that the US could annex Canada as its 51st state.
Trump has also referred to Carney, as well as his predecessor as prime minister, Justin Trudeau, as the "governor" of Canada.
The growing rift has also seen Trump sign an executive order renaming Lake Ontario, a Great Lake between the US and Canada, to "Lake America."

Mark Carney says Canada welcomes EU offer of associate membership despite Trump warning
sources.text:
STRASBOURG, France— Canada is ready to enter a more formal partnership, including associate membership, with the European Union to strengthen sovereignty and resist global pressures, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday as the U.S. president threatened to punish such a move.
Speaking to a half-full European Parliament chamber that belatedly filled up, Carney brushed aside Donald Trump’s late-night warning that any move by the EU to accept Canada as its first associate member would be a “hostile act” that could warrant steep tariffs on Europe, if not outright trade bans.
Instead, Carney took up the call by EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen a day earlier and said he is open to her invitation to move beyond the Canada-Europe Trade Agreement on free trade to establishing what both called an “alliance for the future.”
Von der Leyen, in her state of the union address to Parliament on Wednesday, urged Canada to work toward becoming the first associate member of the EU despite the fact that associate membership is not set out in the 27-country bloc’s framework.
“We welcome this ambition,” Carney said in his Thursday speech after being greeted for the second day on the parliament’s red carpet and posing for selfies with European politicians.
In a later news conference, Carney said Canada is not interested in full EU membership, and “what’s on offer” is a “different framework.” He shrugged off labels, noting von der Leyen had used both terms: alliance and associate membership, adding that the question of what to call it is up to European lawmakers. But the prime minister said he, von der Leyen and several European leaders he informally consulted had embraced the need for a deeper partnership.
“What matters is the substance. What are we actually building together? How do we combine our strengths in a way that serve our people better, protect our fundamental rights, and create prosperity?” Carney said.
The speech signalled that Canada was ready to enter a stronger relationship with the European Union, including associate membership.
As if to pre-empt political critics at home, including Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre who condemned it as a loss of sovereignty, Carney said in his speech that polling shows “an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties.”
Speaking alongside European Parliament President Roberta Metsola, the counterpart to the speaker of the House of Commons who had invited the Canadian leader here, Carney promised transparency as the details get worked out. He rejected the suggestion that it would cost Canada control over critical sectors, saying it would, on the contrary, strengthen sovereignty and fill gaps in strategic areas.
Canadian MPs will have a chance to voice their views. “Of course,” there will be a series of debates in parliamentary committees, Carney said, and “ultimately there will be a vote in the Canadian Parliament for the final structure of the alliance that we’re working on.”
In answer to Trump’s condemnation, Carney said in his speech, “I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival — only with better manners,” drawing laughter and applause in the chamber.
“We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law. Those motivations, combined with our latent hard power, mean we can help to create the next just, stable, and prosperous world order.”
Speaking later to reporters, Carney cocked an eyebrow and briefly flashed a grin when asked to respond to Trump’s characterization of a Canada-European alliance as a potentially “hostile act.”
“This alliance is a positive process,” Carney replied in French. “That’s my response to the American president. It’s a positive thing. A stronger, more resilient, more sovereign Canada will be a more effective partner with the United States. Same would go for the European Union.”
Hours after EU President Ursula von der Leyen proposed an ‘alliance for the future’ with Canada, the U.S. president called it a potentially
Pressed further about whether he fears the alliance with Europe will strain Canada-U.S. relations, Carney avoided mentioning Trump altogether. “I’m interested in the ideas, perspectives and leadership” of “presidents” like von der Leyen, Metsola, or the president of France, Emmanuel Macron, he said. Carney is scheduled to meet Sunday, on the French overseas territory of St-Pierre-et Miquelon off Newfoundland’s south coast, with Macron ahead of next week’s United Nations meetings.
Trump’s global tariffs, his war of choice in Iran, and his courting of China, Russia and other authoritarian leaders, along with his musings about annexing Canada as a 51st state or the Danish territory of Greenland as American territory, have fuelled widespread anxiety among other U.S. trading partners and allies.
Like his Davos speech nine months ago, Carney’s address was peppered with literary and metaphorical references, this time to German writer-philosopher and statesman Johann Wolfgang Goethe, Canada’s blood ties to Europe born of wartime sacrifices, and an extended forest analogy for how countries can learn to survive killer storms.
Where the Davos speech in January at the World Economic Forum called on middle powers to band together to form coalitions to resist superpowers like the U.S., Russia and China which spurn rules and are upending the international order, the Strasbourg speech suggested such a coalition already exists between Canada and Europe, and should be deepened.
“We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals,” he said.
“Canada and Europe are not bound by geography, even though our Danish friends know that we do share a 3,000 km border in the Arctic; we are bound by an affinity — elective, chosen, and renewed, and stronger for being so.”
“A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies,” the prime minister said. “An alliance not defined by what we oppose, but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability. An alliance that builds resilience for what it allows us to do for our citizens, and our citizens to do for themselves. An alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices. Open enough that others can join. Principled enough that our strength reinforces international law rather than replaces it.”
Mark Carney will have to sell the notion to Parliament and the wider public amid difficult political realities.
Carney said his objective for “a deeper partnership” with Europe is “collective resilience.”
The prime minister said there is “mutual advantage” in combining strategic capabilities in key sectors to address vulnerabilities and sustain economic and national security in the face of geopolitical uncertainty.
“Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep co-operation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space, and payments,” Carney’s prepared text said.
He spelled out how those sectors could be leveraged.
“Europe brings market power. Research depth. Advanced manufacturing. The ability to set standards that the world frequently adopts,” he said, pointing to the “rearm Europe” project that is rapidly building up a stronger defence industrial base. Canada’s participation in that program, called SAFE, was agreed to last year, the first non-European country to join.
On the other hand, Carney said Canada offers “energy at huge scale and in every form” the clean energy transition requires, along with “one of the world’s largest endowments of critical minerals, deep capabilities in space, AI and quantum, amongst the strongest banking systems in the world, and the most expert pension capital. We have unique Arctic geography, and privileged access to both Atlantic and Pacific networks.
Time, Carney suggested, was of the essence. “We should build on each other’s strengths — deliberately, systematically, and rapidly.”
The Canada-Europe free trade agreement, and a defence and strategic partnership launched last year are “not yet equal to the ferocity of the changing climate, nor is it moving fast enough to match the speed of the upheaval,” he said.
The two should move toward “seamless, digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services,” ease the ability of young people to “live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic” Ocean and advance other initiatives.

Also Read: Trump wanted Canada closer to America; Ottawa is now flirting with the EU instead
Carney said plainly what he was proposing: deeper Canada-Europe integration across trade, defense, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, energy, space, research and financial services to make both sides less vulnerable to economic and geopolitical pressure.
“I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival — only with better manners,” he said. “We do not seek power to dominate others."
Carney said the goal instead is to build Canada’s resilience so that no country can control its markets, undermine its sovereignty or dictate its choices.
For generations, Canada built its economy around integration with the United States. Trump’s tariffs, demands for economic concessions and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state are now driving Ottawa to reduce that dependence and seek a deeper economic, security and political relationship across the Atlantic.
Europe offers Canada another path
Von der Leyen proposed making Canada the EU’s first associate member — a status that does not currently exist in the bloc’s treaties and would have to be created. She said Europe wants to take its relationship with Canada to “the highest level possible.”
Carney, sitting in the front row of the European Parliament chamber, nodded and rose to embrace von der Leyen as lawmakers gave the proposal a standing ovation.
Also Read: Canada invited to become EU bloc’s first associate member
This time, Europe is offering Canada another path.
Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU should move beyond their existing free trade agreement and create an “Alliance for the Future” encompassing a “common prosperity and economic security space.”
Carney will host EU leaders for a Canada-EU summit in Montreal on Oct. 29-30, where the two sides are expected to discuss the proposed new relationship in more detail.
Canada sends roughly 70% of its exports to the United States, making it highly exposed to Trump’s tariffs. Ottawa has retaliated and rejected demands Carney says threaten Canadian sovereignty. Europe took a different path, shelving retaliation and accepting tariffs of up to 15% on most EU exports to the U.S.
Carney has rallied ‘middle powers’
Carney has repeatedly urged middle powers to resist that kind of economic coercion. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, he warned that when countries negotiate alone with a dominant power, “we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered.”
Trump rebuked him the next day.
Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the EU, said Wednesday that Canada is not seeking full EU membership because that would require surrendering some sovereignty. Instead, Ottawa wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to Europe while increasing Canada’s independence.
Exactly what associate membership would mean remains to be negotiated.
Canada has already taken a major step toward European integration. This year it became the first non-European country to join the EU’s 150-billion-euro ($173-billion) SAFE defense procurement program, giving Canadian companies access to joint procurement as Europe increases defense spending.
The two sides have also discussed closer cooperation on energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and digital trade.
“The policies and rhetoric of the Trump administration are clearly pushing both Canada and the EU to imagine a world without strong U.S. leadership and to act accordingly,” said Daniel Béland, a political-science professor at McGill University in Montreal.
Nelson Wiseman, a professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Carney’s handling of Trump has heightened European interest in the Canadian leader.
“Carney’s shrewdness in dealing with Trump has captured Europe’s attention,” Wiseman said.
Washington will be watching
Wiseman said Europeans have long regarded Canada as a country that understands the United States particularly well because of their deep economic and political ties. Carney’s willingness to resist Trump rather than quickly accept Washington’s demands has reinforced that perception, he said.
Béland said Carney may avoid naming Trump on Thursday while leaving little doubt about the target of his broader argument.
“He knows that, beyond Europe, the world will be watching, including the White House,” Béland said.

Carney’s speech came one day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen used her state of the union address to the European Parliament to open the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member” of the EU. Carney said he welcomed the move, but during a news conference in Strasbourg, France, following the speech, he also said Canadian members of Parliament will be given the chance to debate and vote on whatever alliance is ultimately proposed. “Yes, we will have a series of debates, I’m sure, in Parliament, relevant committees, and ultimately there will be a vote in the Canadian Parliament for the final structure of the alliance that we’re working on,” Carney said, while standing alongside Roberta Metsola, president of the European Parliament. “The next important point is the summit, European-Canada summit in Montreal at the 29th and 30th of October, but it will all roll out transparently. It’s an exciting time because this is an opportunity to speak for Canada. Make Canada stronger, more sovereign, more independent, more prosperous, more sustainable.” A similar debate will happen in the European Parliament. “We look forward and positively at new opportunities with allies such as Canada, with whom we have had partnerships and alliances, call them what you will, for hundreds of years,” Metsola said. “The overwhelmingly positive reaction of members in plenary just a few moments ago will be reflected in a similar reaction in the committees. Of that, I have no doubt.” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez reacted to Carney’s speech by sharing a picture on social media of the EU flag with a red maple leaf just off to the left of the circle of 12 yellow stars. The circle is meant to represent unity and harmony among Europe’s people. The circle is meant to represent unity and harmony among Europe’s people. Carney said Thursday the “nomenclature” of a new partnership would be determined by the EU but the substance of the arrangement is more important than its name. That substance is still being developed, but Carney said Canada and Europe should forge deeper ties on critical minerals, defence, artificial intelligence and energy security. He said the two partners should look at allowing young people to live, work and study on either side of the Atlantic, and creating an integrated market for financial services. Metsola said this could include Canada joining Erasmus+, a program that facilities student exchanges between member countries. “If you ask our young people what they associate the European Union with, I would tell you Erasmus is the first thing they mentioned. Horizon is the second thing they mention in terms of opportunities that with Canada could only get bigger,” she said. Horizon Europe is an EU program that funds various research and innovation projects. The program’s budget for 2021-2027 is about $150 billion. Carney did not mention U.S. President Donald Trump by name in his speech, though he alluded to strained relations between both Canada and Europe and the American administration. “We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy, share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication,” Carney said. “We hold common values, for which we have always fought, and in whose defence we must always remain vigilant.” Trump said Wednesday he views the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU as a possible “hostile act” and threatened to impose more tariffs on Europe. Carney said a deeper alliance will make Canada a “better partner with the United States.” “Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak, no one going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike agreements internationally,” Carney said. That was a nod to the recent breakdown in trade talks between Canada and the United States. Carney suspended negotiations just before a U.S.-set tariff deadline in August, and he said the U.S. had made demands Canada refused, including restrictions on Canada’s protections for French, and on its ability to make trade deals with other countries. In his address, Carney also sketched out the limits of the proposed arrangement with the EU. “I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival -- only with better manners,” he said. “We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.” After Carney’s speech, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre shared a video on social media of his Wednesday caucus address from Penticton, B.C. In it, he said Canadians should decide the future direction of the country. “We will continue to support co-operation with our European allies, of course, that is the Conservative tradition ... The prime minister, however, needs to get his story straight. He says he wants a possible associate membership or a unique alliance or whatever else he is secretly negotiating with the EU,” Poilievre said in his speech. “But Conservatives are clear. While we support free trade and continued NATO co-operation with our European allies, Conservatives say no EU taxes, no EU laws, and no EU open border policies on immigration in Canada.” Ten of 27 EU countries still haven’t ratified a trade deal with Canada that has been in place provisionally for nine years. Canadian businesses have not taken up market access provided to them in Europe to the same extent that European industries have in Canada. Carney received standing ovations at the beginning and end of his speech from about two-thirds of the European parliamentarians. Terry Reintke, co-leader of the Greens in the European Parliament said the day before Carney’s speech that she hoped to see him more often in the Parliament. She wore a Sidney Crosby Team Canada jersey as she sat in the front row for Carney’s speech. The Greens hold seven per cent of the seats in the EU Parliament. Not all parliamentarians were as receptive. As Carney approached the podium to begin his speech, one of the European parliamentarians welcomed him with a chant of “USA, USA.” The prime minister chuckled in response. The Fed raises interest rates. And, EU proposes Canada become an 'associate member'
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
The Federal Reserve unanimously voted to raise interest rates yesterday for the first time in more than three years, increasing the benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%. The hike makes it more expensive to borrow money, grow a business or carry a credit card balance. Inflation has risen amid the war in Iran, driving up the price of gasoline and diesel fuel. While higher interest rates won't immediately lower prices, they demonstrate the Fed's commitment to restoring price stability, despite repeated pressure from President Trump to lower interest rates.
- 🎧 Trump's demands for lower rates came up frequently during Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference yesterday, NPR's Alina Selyukh tells Up First. Like his predecessor, Jerome Powell, Warsh didn't engage and reiterated the Fed's independence. Selyukh says the Fed faces the challenge of slowing the economy without tipping the country into a recession. The Fed does not control key drivers of inflation, such as tariff policies, nor does it control wages, which have been stagnant for months. Selyukh says workers' paychecks have been losing buying power, and Warsh hopes stable prices will help families cope with inflation.
Rising gas prices have sparked protests around the world, including in Syria, the Philippines and Indonesia. The price surge comes as Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, faces a renewed war in Yemen against the Iranian-backed Houthis.
- 🎧 NPR's Aya Batrawy says the escalation in fighting has challenged energy supplies. Last month, Saudi Arabia's oil output fell to around 6.2 million barrels a day — down from 11 million before the war in Iran began. There's also a large human toll: The fighting this month between the Houthis and Saudi-backed groups has displaced more than 100,000 people, according to the U.N. Trump remains focused on the U.S. conflict with Iran and so far shows no intention of striking the Houthis, as the U.S. did last year. A Saudi official, speaking anonymously in order to discuss security matters, confirmed to NPR a recent meeting between U.S. officials and the Houthis in Oman.
The European Union has proposed making Canada its first-ever "associate member." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the proposal for the new model of membership during her annual speech to the EU Parliament in Strasbourg, France. In his own address to the EU Parliament this morning, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney emphasized how much the EU and Canada have in common and said that "Europe and Canada are stronger together."
- 🎧 Canada and the EU have felt bullied by the Trump administration over tariffs, threats to abandon NATO and proposals to take over Greenland or make Canada the 51st state, NPR's Eleanor Beardsley says. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said this morning that he welcomes working more closely with Canada, but would need to see what being an associate member means. Beardsley says many probably view Canada's potential EU membership as mostly symbolic. When asked about it yesterday, Trump said the concept is laughable and could be seen as a hostile move.
Deep dive
A bill championed by crypto executives and President Trump failed to pass a Senate vote this week. The Clarity Act would have established the first regulations for the crypto sector in U.S. history. A version of the bill passed the House last year. Now, the bill's future is uncertain as the crypto industry and its backers must weigh their options for another attempt. Here are some key things to know about the Clarity Act:
- 🪙 The act aimed to formally divide crypto oversight between the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, but more control would be given to the smaller regulator, CFTC.
- 🪙 Critics argue that granting the CFTC the bulk of the control allows the crypto sector to evade heavy regulatory scrutiny. Industry executives deny the accusation.
- 🪙 A key sticking point for some Democratic opponents is the concern that the ethics clause intended to prevent presidents and elected officials from profiting from the crypto industry while in office fails to adequately prevent conflicts of interest.
- 🪙 The bill isn't dead yet, but it is likely to face a tough time passing this year with midterms approaching. If Democrats control the House or Senate after the elections, passing the bill could become even more challenging.
Behind the story
by Chiara Eisner, Investigative Correspondent
For decades, NASA's Goddard facility in Maryland has been famous for one thing: engineering spacecraft that try to answer big questions. Questions like: Are we alone? How many other planets might be able to support life? Why is the universe expanding?
It takes billions of dollars, custom-built rooms and teams of experienced engineers to make the telescopes and satellites that can shed some light on those questions. But last year, NASA's management started forcing engineers out of those specialized labs. In some cases, NASA leaders gave them less than a week to pack up their devices and designate what equipment they would have to lose in order to fit into the smaller spaces they were told to move to. Other times, sources told me, the teams' equipment was moved — and even donated to other institutions — without the scientists' knowledge.
After lawmakers asked the government's independent watchdog office overseeing NASA to investigate the impact of those moves, the agency in June found that those relocations hadn't hurt ongoing projects and would "not impact NASA's anticipated missions."
But I spoke with seven current and former NASA scientists and engineers at Goddard who said that wasn't true. Some of NASA's most ambitious projects, like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, launched in August, were affected, NPR found.
Experts told me that it signals danger for NASA's future.
"That only adds a whole lot of risk to an already risky endeavor," said Jack Kiraly, chief of advocacy at The Planetary Society, a nonprofit that champions space science and exploration. "These are potentially billions of dollars worth of taxpayer investment. We don't do ourselves any favors by putting the people that make this happen in precarious situations."
3 things to know before you go
- Researchers have developed a new way to implant lab-grown human brain cells into mice, helping them to better research complex neurological diseases. But as the technology grows more complex, so do the questions surrounding the ethics of this process.
- Author Annie Dillard, who wrote several books including 1974's Pulitzer Prize-winning Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, has died at age 81.
- When Tracy Zito's young son got caught in a current in Lake Michigan, she feared the worst as she struggled to pull him back to shore. An unsung hero suddenly appeared beside her and brought her son to safety. More than 15 years later, Zito still feels tears in her eyes when she recalls this courageous act.

Carney calls for closer Canada-EU alliance to defend values
Published in News & Features
Prime Minister Mark Carney called for a closer alliance between Canada and the European Union in a bid to establish a bulwark strong enough to ward off intimidation from world powers like the U.S. and China that could threaten their sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Carney welcomed a speech made by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, when she proposed that Canada become the first “associate member” of the E.U., noting that Canadians support closer ties. President Donald Trump threatened a new round of tariffs against the bloc if he deems the new relationship to be harmful to the U.S.
“We do not seek power to dominate others,” Carney told European lawmakers in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday. “On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”
Trump has demolished the transatlantic relationship, calling into question American security guarantees for Europe and starting trade wars with both Brussels and Ottawa. The E.U. and Canada have been seeking to form alliances with like-minded partners to band together and oppose the pressure tactics and intimidation of the world’s dominant economies, particularly the U.S. and China.
“Europe and Canada are each strong,” he added. “Europe and Canada are even stronger together.”
Carney’s government, economically shaken by a trade war with the U.S., has made it a top priority to forge deeper partnerships with allies, including the E.U. After U.S.-Canada talks ended last month, Trump imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion of goods imported from Canada, and Carney soon retaliated with tariffs on a roughly equal amount of U.S.-made products.
Asked about Trump’s criticism of the proposed alliance, Carney said that the move toward an enhanced relationship was a positive development that will make Canada a “better partner with the U.S.” He also said there would be debates and a vote in Canadian parliament on the final structure of any alliance, stressing that “we’re at the start of a road.”
Trade between the E.U. and Canada jumped to €130 billion ($149 billion) last year, following the provisional implementation of a free-trade agreement in 2017. The E.U. is Canada’s second-largest trading partner after the U.S.
Von der Leyen was vague on what associate membership would entail, but said the two regions would seek closer cooperation on manufacturing, tech, defense and energy, and cited the Arctic as a “flagship joint project.”
Among the proposals outlined by Carney were greater cooperation in critical materials, defense industrial capacity, AI, space and payments. Noting that Canada has deposits of more than 34 critical minerals, he said that an E.U.-Canada alliance could “help fill Europe’s need for reliable supply, Canada’s need for advanced processing capabilities.”
In addition, he said that Canada and Europe should also explore the creation of an integrated market for financial services. He also called for Canada’s inclusion in the E.U. program that allows students to study in the bloc’s universities.
Canada’s government has made clear it’s eager to boost economic ties with the rest of the world, including the E.U., in a multi-year strategic shift to reorient trade flows more to the east and west, rather than being primarily focused southbound toward the U.S.
“We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defense of human dignity, individual freedom, and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication,” he said. “We believe that our prosperity grows when it is shared. This is a sharing of choice not coincidence.”
The proposal could cause problems in both Canada and in Europe. Previous ideas, including a proposal to offer a “light” membership to Ukraine was shot down by both Kyiv, who feared it would be detrimental to full membership, and by a number of capitals, who insisted the lengthy, merit-based accession process had to be the same for all.
The proposal to formalize a relationship with the E.U. was panned by Canada’s Conservative Party, which is the main federal opposition group. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wrote on social media earlier this week that “We will NEVER be the 51st U.S. state. And we will NEVER be the 28th E.U. state.”
A recent Abacus Data survey found 80% of Canadians support closer integration with the E.U. on issues such as foreign policy, defense and economic opportunities, up six percentage points since February. Support for full E.U. membership is weaker, with 49% of saying they’re in favor of it.
“The objective is not self-sufficiency. It is collective resilience,” Carney said. “This mutual advantage is at the core of the case for a deeper partnership between Canada and Europe.”

Poilievre speculated that the alliance likely isn't a military alliance, as 30 European countries and Canada are already part of NATO.
"That leaves very little left for him to sign. You know, if he's talking about forcing Canadians to pay taxes to Brussels bureaucrats or to follow European Union laws that we never voted on, or God forbid, to bring European policies for immigration, that would be a disaster for Canada," Poilievre said.
He added that Conservatives would "never support forcing Canadians to pay European taxes, follow European laws, or welcome European policy on immigration that would further overwhelm our hospitals, housing, and jobs."
Ultimately, Poilievre demanded transparency from the federal government and asserted that Canada, as a nation, needs to retain sovereignty over its borders, immigration, taxes, and laws."That's sovereignty, and that is what we will, as conservatives, defend. But we're all left speculating because so far all we have are leaks from the Canadian and European governments to the Wall Street Journal, combined with wordplay by the prime minister; he won't show up in Canada's House of Commons to answer any questions."When asked whether joining the EU in this capacity could have been planned with Carney, who rejected a deal with the U.S. moments after agreeing to it, Poilievre said there's no way to know, as Carney hasn't been transparent with what the deal with the U.S. entailed.
"So we're all left wondering what he's talking about."
"The way to put that all the rest is for the prime minister to just release the text of the agreement that he had accepted, and then turned around and rejected it," he said. "He won't tell us. He won't show us what's in that agreement. So it's very hard for me to comment on whether it was a good or bad deal."
Poilievre noted that the details of the deal have gone beyond the point of confidentiality, as both sides of the government have commented "very openly" on what the trade talks said, although those reports are conflicting.
"He can release the text, and then let Canadians judge whether it was a deal that he should have walked away from," Poilievre said.
The Prime Minister's Office, Global Affairs Canada and the office of the International Trade Minister have yet to respond to Juno News' requests for clarity on what "associate membership with the EU" entails.
